title: Overview and justification
body:
This is an advanced course on creativity: not what creativity is, but what it is worth. By the end you will be able to appraise creativity as a graduate attribute that drives innovation and enterprise, integrate creative self-regulation into your own development, and critique how creativity operates in scholarly interpretation and debate.

You already treat creativity as a usable academic skill. The question now is more demanding. Why do disciplines, employers and research communities prize creativity so highly, and how do you exercise it deliberately in your own work and judgement? This course takes creativity seriously as a professional and intellectual attribute.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: appraise creativity as a graduate attribute that drives innovation and enterprise
integrate creative self-regulation into your own academic development
critique how creativity operates in scholarly interpretation and debate.

title: In real academic practice
body: Creativity is named explicitly among the graduate attributes that disciplines and employers look for, alongside adaptability and flexibility. It is also the engine of original scholarship, where new readings and syntheses move a field forward. Treat this course as being about the creativity your own degree and future work will reward, not creativity in the abstract.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three lessons. First, creativity as a graduate attribute: why innovation and enterprise are prized, and how creativity relates to adaptability. Second, creative self-regulation: how you monitor and amend your own strategies as a self-directed learner. Third, creativity in scholarly discourse: how imagination and interpretation open up debate around a source. Work through them in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you will rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You will rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they are not marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they do not count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you will find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

title: Orientation
body: Ask what a degree is for, and one answer is the graduate who leaves it: someone employers and disciplines describe through a set of attributes. Creativity sits near the top of that list. This lesson treats creativity not as a classroom skill but as a professional attribute, and asks why it is valued so highly and what it has to do with adaptability and enterprise.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are an experienced student, and you have used creative methods in your work already. The task now is to stand back and appraise creativity as an attribute: to say what makes it valuable beyond any single assignment, and to argue its worth in the terms your discipline and your future field would use.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: appraise why creativity ranks among the graduate attributes that disciplines and employers prize
relate creativity to adaptability and flexibility in professional problem-solving
articulate how creativity as innovation shows up in {{context}} and your future work.

title: Concept: definition
body:
In the language of graduate attributes, creativity means thinking innovatively in order to solve problems. It is listed as a prized capability precisely because the problems that matter rarely come with a settled method; they ask for something new. In this sense creativity is not decoration but a form of problem-solving under uncertainty.

Two attributes sit close beside it. Adaptability is the readiness to change approach when circumstances shift, and flexibility is the capacity to hold more than one option open. Creativity supplies the new option; adaptability and flexibility decide when to reach for it. Together they describe a graduate who can meet an unfamiliar problem and make progress on it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a problem in your own field that has no routine solution. What would it mean to meet it creatively, and how would adaptability change the option you first reached for?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Creativity earns its place among the graduate attributes because it generates workable options for problems that have no settled method, and because that habit transfers from study to professional life. You can now appraise creativity as an attribute, relate it to adaptability and flexibility, and articulate how it shows up in your own field. The next lesson turns creativity inward, onto how you regulate your own learning.

title: Orientation
body: Self-regulated learners do not simply work hard; they watch how their work is going and change it when it falters. That act of changing approach is more creative than it looks. This lesson treats creativity as something you turn on your own learning: monitoring a strategy, judging when it is failing, and devising a better one.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You already plan and review your own study. The advanced move is to treat strategy itself as a creative problem. Rather than persisting with a method because it is familiar, you appraise it against results and generate an alternative, deliberately, as part of how you regulate your learning.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: integrate creative strategy-switching into the self-regulated learning cycle
appraise when a learning strategy is failing and justify amending it
devise an amended approach when a chosen method is not working in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Self-regulated learning runs as a cycle: you plan an approach, carry it out, monitor how it is going, and reflect on the result before planning again. The point most often missed is the monitoring. If a strategy is not working effectively, the self-regulating learner does not simply try harder; they amend it, choosing another that might work better.

That amendment is a creative act. Devising a different route to the same goal, under constraints you now understand better, is problem-solving turned on your own practice. Creativity here is not inspiration; it is the disciplined generation of a better option when the monitoring tells you the current one has stalled.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a study strategy you have kept using even though it was not really working. What was the monitoring telling you, and what amended approach could you have devised instead?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Self-regulated learning becomes creative at the moment of amendment: when honest monitoring shows a strategy has stalled and you devise a better route rather than simply trying harder. You can now place strategy-switching in the cycle, appraise when a method is failing, and devise an alternative in your own study. The final lesson turns to creativity in scholarship itself.

title: Orientation
body: Scholarship advances when someone reads a source in a way others had not, and makes that reading defensible. That is creativity at the heart of academic work: not invention from nothing, but imaginative interpretation that opens a settled text back up for debate. This lesson examines how creativity operates in scholarly discourse, and how you exercise it responsibly.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can already engage critically with sources. The advanced move is to see the creative dimension of interpretation: to recognise that an original reading is a contribution, to appraise how others have opened up a discourse, and to justify your own reading as one voice among several rather than the last word.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: critique how creativity and imagination feature in scholarly interpretations
appraise an interpretation by opening up the discourse around it
justify your own reading of a source in {{context}} as one creative voice in a debate.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Analysis, in scholarship, is more than taking an argument apart. To analyse an interpretation is to see how a scholar has read their material imaginatively, and to weigh that reading against others. Writers on creativity itself make the point: some tie creativity to the development of imagination, others to cognitive development, and the discipline holds these interpretations in tension rather than settling them.

Opening up the discourse means refusing to treat any one source as the final account. A less experienced researcher might take a single authoritative text as settled. The more creative move is to read it as one contribution, ask what it assumes and leaves out, and place your own interpretation alongside it with reasons. Creativity here is disciplined imagination, answerable to evidence and to the debate.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a source you have treated as the settled account in your field. What would it take to read it as one interpretation among several, and what reading of your own might you argue?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Creativity in scholarship is disciplined imagination: reading a source as one contestable interpretation, opening up the discourse around it, and justifying a reading of your own against the evidence and the alternatives. You can now critique how creativity features in interpretation, appraise an interpretation by opening up its discourse, and defend your own voice in a debate. With the earlier lessons, you can now treat creativity as a professional attribute, a mode of self-regulation, and a scholarly practice.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Creativity is no longer only a study skill: it is an attribute you can argue for and exercise deliberately. You can appraise creativity as a graduate attribute that drives innovation and enterprise, and say why it transfers beyond any single task. You can integrate creative self-regulation into your own learning, amending a strategy when honest monitoring shows it has stalled. And you can critique how creativity works in scholarship, opening up the discourse around a source and justifying a reading of your own. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, creativity is something you exercise in every advanced task. Each problem with no routine solution, each strategy you amend rather than repeat, each interpretation you open up and argue, is the attribute at work. It is also what research and professional life reward: the capacity to generate and defend new options under uncertainty travels well beyond your degree.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Creativity as an attribute
body: Four facets of creativity as a graduate attribute. Review each card.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Innovation
_items.subtitle: Solving the new problem
_items.text: Creativity is prized because it generates options where no method is given. Thinking innovatively turns an unfamiliar problem into one you can make progress on.

_items.title: Enterprise
_items.subtitle: Acting on an idea
_items.text: An idea has professional value only when someone carries it into practice. Enterprise is creativity put to work: shaping a proposal, a project or a venture from a possibility others had not seen.

_items.title: Adaptability
_items.subtitle: Changing approach
_items.text: Creativity and adaptability are siblings. When an approach stops working, the adaptable graduate does not persist out of habit; they devise another route, which is a creative act in itself.

_items.title: Transfer
_items.subtitle: Beyond one task
_items.text: What makes creativity an attribute, rather than a one-off, is that it travels. The habit of generating and testing new options carries from an essay to a workplace problem to an unforeseen situation.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two final-year students are asked, in a careers task, to describe how creativity features in their intended profession.

{{learner-a}} writes that creativity means coming up with original ideas, and that creative people are an asset to any employer. The claim is true but generic. It names creativity as a good thing without saying what problem it solves or how it would show up in the work, so it would read the same on any application in any field.

{{learner-b}} identifies a recurring problem in the field that has no routine solution, and argues that this is exactly where creativity earns its place: generating a workable option, then adapting it as constraints become clear. Creativity is tied to a concrete problem, linked to adaptability, and expressed as enterprise rather than as a personality trait.

Both value creativity. Only {{learner-b}} appraises it as an attribute: named, located in real problems, and argued for in the terms the profession would recognise.

title: Appraising the attribute
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These prompts help you argue creativity as an attribute rather than praise it in general. Try them on your own field.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I named the kind of problem that calls for creativity here, rather than praising creativity in general?
Have I said what creativity actually produces: a new, workable option?
Have I linked creativity to adaptability, the readiness to change the option as things shift?
Have I shown creativity as enterprise, an idea carried into practice, not just had?
Have I argued its value in the terms my discipline or profession would use?
Could I defend why this attribute travels beyond the single task in front of me?

title: Formative check: why creativity is prized
displayTitle: Which reason best justifies ranking creativity among the graduate attributes disciplines and employers prize?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which reason best justifies ranking creativity among graduate attributes?

_items.text: Because it generates workable options for problems that have no settled method.
_items.feedback: Yes. Creativity is problem-solving under uncertainty, which is why it is valued.

_items.text: Because it makes written work longer and more varied.
_items.feedback: Length and variety are not what the attribute names.

_items.text: Because it lets a graduate avoid difficult problems altogether.
_items.feedback: Creativity meets hard problems; it does not avoid them.

_items.text: Because it is a fixed personality trait that cannot be developed.
_items.feedback: Creativity is treated as a developable attribute, not a fixed trait.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Creativity is prized because it produces workable options where no method is given.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what creativity does with a problem that has no routine solution.
_incorrect.final: Creativity ranks among graduate attributes because it generates workable options under uncertainty. The other options mistake it for length, avoidance or a fixed trait.

title: Formative check: appraising versus praising
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's account an appraisal of creativity rather than generic praise?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's account an appraisal rather than praise?

_items.text: They tied creativity to a concrete problem and linked it to adaptability and enterprise.
_items.feedback: Yes. Locating creativity in a real problem is what turns praise into appraisal.

_items.text: They said creativity is an asset to any employer.
_items.feedback: That is the generic praise the first student offered.

_items.text: They wrote a longer answer than the first student.
_items.feedback: Length is not what made the difference.

_items.text: They described creativity as an inborn personality trait.
_items.feedback: Treating it as a trait is the opposite of appraising it as an attribute.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student located creativity in a concrete problem and linked it to adaptability and enterprise.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student did beyond calling creativity valuable.
_incorrect.final: The appraisal tied creativity to a real problem and to adaptability and enterprise. Generic praise, length and trait-talk do none of that.

title: Formative check: creativity in your field
displayTitle: You are arguing that creativity matters in {{context}}. Which move best shows creativity as a graduate attribute?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best shows creativity as a graduate attribute?

_items.text: Naming a real problem in {{context}} that has no routine solution and showing how a new option would address it.
_items.feedback: Yes. That locates creativity in a concrete problem in {{context}}, which is how the attribute is argued.

_items.text: Stating that people in {{context}} should be more creative.
_items.feedback: An exhortation is not an argument for the attribute.

_items.text: Listing creativity among your personal strengths without an example.
_items.feedback: A claim with no problem attached is generic.

_items.text: Avoiding any problem that looks too difficult.
_items.feedback: Creativity meets hard problems rather than avoiding them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, naming a problem with no routine solution and showing a new option argues creativity as an attribute.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that ties creativity to a concrete problem in {{context}}.
_incorrect.final: The attribute is argued by locating it in a real problem in {{context}} and a new option for it. Exhortation, bare lists and avoidance do not.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The self-regulation cycle
body: The self-regulated learning cycle, stage by stage. The creative move lives at monitoring and amending.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal how the cycle turns.

_items.title: Choose an approach
_items.body: You set a goal and pick a strategy for reaching it, drawing on what has worked before and what the task seems to need.

_items.title: Put it into practice
_items.body: You carry the strategy out in earnest, giving it a fair trial rather than abandoning it at the first difficulty.

_items.title: Watch how it is going
_items.body: You track results against the goal. This is the pivot of the cycle: honest monitoring is what tells you whether the strategy is earning its place.

_items.title: Devise a better route
_items.body: If the strategy is not working effectively, you do not just persist. You generate an alternative that the monitoring suggests might work better. This is the creative move.

_items.title: Carry the lesson forward
_items.body: You review what the change achieved, so the next plan is better informed. The cycle begins again, now with sharper judgement.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students realise, three weeks into a module, that their usual way of preparing is not working.

{{learner-a}} notices the method is yielding little but keeps going, reasoning that more hours will fix it. The strategy is never questioned, only intensified. By the assessment, {{learner-a}} is exhausted and no further forward, having monitored the symptom without amending the cause.

{{learner-b}} treats the stall as information. The monitoring says the current method is not working, so {{learner-b}} asks what, specifically, it is failing to do, and devises a different approach aimed at that gap. The new strategy is given a fair trial and reviewed in turn. The problem is solved creatively, from within {{learner-b}}'s own regulation.

Both students saw the same warning sign. Only {{learner-b}} answered it by amending the strategy rather than merely repeating it.

title: Regulating your strategy
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves turn monitoring into creative amendment. Try them the next time a strategy stalls.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I set a clear goal that lets me tell whether my strategy is working?
Have I given the strategy a fair trial before judging it?
Have I monitored results honestly, rather than assuming effort equals progress?
When a strategy stalls, have I identified what exactly it is failing to do?
Have I devised a genuinely different approach, not just more of the same?
Have I reviewed what the change achieved, so my next plan is better informed?

title: Formative check: where switching belongs
displayTitle: At which point in the self-regulated learning cycle can creative strategy-switching best be justified?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: At which point in the cycle can creative strategy-switching best be justified?

_items.text: At monitoring and amending, when results show the current strategy has stalled.
_items.feedback: Yes. The creative switch belongs where monitoring reveals a stall.

_items.text: Only at the very start, before any strategy is chosen.
_items.feedback: Switching responds to results, which only appear once a strategy is running.

_items.text: At no point; the cycle requires sticking to one strategy throughout.
_items.feedback: The cycle depends on amending a strategy that is not working.

_items.text: Only after the course is over, when reflecting in general.
_items.feedback: Amendment happens during the cycle, not only afterwards.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Creative strategy-switching belongs at monitoring and amending.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. When does the cycle give you the information that a switch is needed?
_incorrect.final: The switch belongs at monitoring and amending, where results reveal a stall. It is not a start-only, never, or after-the-fact move.

title: Formative check: amending versus intensifying
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that the first did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that the first did not?

_items.text: Treated the stall as information and amended the strategy, rather than only intensifying it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Amending in response to monitoring is the creative, self-regulating move.

_items.text: Worked more hours on the same method.
_items.feedback: That is what the first student did; it is intensifying, not amending.

_items.text: Abandoned the module when the method faltered.
_items.feedback: Neither student abandoned the work; the point is how they changed strategy.

_items.text: Waited until the assessment to review the method.
_items.feedback: The second student reviewed during the cycle, not only at the end.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student amended the strategy once the monitoring showed it had stalled.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student changed, rather than how hard they worked.
_incorrect.final: The second student treated the stall as information and amended the strategy. Intensifying, abandoning or waiting are not that.

title: Formative check: amending in your study
displayTitle: A study method you rely on in {{context}} has clearly stopped working. Which response best shows creative self-regulation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response best shows creative self-regulation?

_items.text: Work out what the method is failing to do, then devise a different approach aimed at that gap.
_items.feedback: Yes. Diagnosing the gap and devising an alternative is creative self-regulation in {{context}}.

_items.text: Put in more hours on the same method until it pays off.
_items.feedback: Intensifying a stalled method is not amending it.

_items.text: Switch subjects so the method is no longer needed.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the task does not solve the strategy problem.

_items.text: Keep the method because it has worked in {{context}} before.
_items.feedback: Past success does not help once the monitoring shows it has stalled.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you diagnose what the method is failing to do and devise a better route.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that changes the strategy in response to the stall.
_incorrect.final: Creative self-regulation diagnoses the gap and devises a different approach. More hours, avoidance or loyalty to the old method do not.

definition: A reasoned reading of a source that goes beyond what it plainly states to argue what it means.
extendedDefinition: In scholarship, an interpretation is a creative contribution: it reads material imaginatively, then defends that reading against evidence and against rival readings in the field.
example: Reading a study as evidence about imagination, rather than only about test scores, is an interpretation others may contest.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two postgraduates discuss the same influential paper on creativity in education.

{{learner-a}} summarises the paper's interpretation faithfully and treats it as established: this is what the literature says about creativity, so this is the position to adopt. The reading is accurate, but it is closed. No other interpretation is admitted, and {{learner-a}}'s own voice never enters; the discourse is reported, not opened.

{{learner-b}} reads the same paper as one interpretation among several. One scholar ties creativity to imagination, another to cognitive development, and {{learner-b}} asks what each reading assumes and what it leaves out. Then {{learner-b}} advances a reading of their own, argued from the evidence and placed explicitly against the others. The discourse has been opened up.

Both understood the paper. Only {{learner-b}} treated interpretation as creative and contestable, and justified a voice of their own within the debate.

title: Opening up an interpretation
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These moves open a source up for debate rather than closing it down. Try them on a key source in your field.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I read the source as one interpretation, rather than as the settled account?
Have I identified what the interpretation assumes and what it leaves out?
Have I set it against at least one rival reading in the field?
Have I recognised the imaginative move the scholar made, not only their conclusion?
Have I advanced a reading of my own, argued from evidence?
Can I justify my reading as a contribution to the debate, not the last word on it?

title: Formative check: interpretation as creative
displayTitle: Which account best justifies calling scholarly interpretation creative?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which account best justifies calling scholarly interpretation creative?

_items.text: It reads material imaginatively to argue what it means, then defends that reading against evidence and rival readings.
_items.feedback: Yes. Interpretation is disciplined imagination, answerable to evidence.

_items.text: It invents findings that the source does not contain.
_items.feedback: Creative interpretation is answerable to evidence; it does not fabricate.

_items.text: It restates the source's conclusion as accurately as possible.
_items.feedback: Accurate restatement is description, not interpretation.

_items.text: It avoids taking any position so as to stay neutral.
_items.feedback: Interpretation advances a reading; neutrality is not the point.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Creative interpretation reads imaginatively and defends the reading against evidence and alternatives.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Creative here means disciplined imagination, not invention or mere restatement.
_incorrect.final: Interpretation is creative because it argues a reading imaginatively yet answerably. Fabrication, restatement and neutrality are not that.

title: Formative check: opening up the discourse
displayTitle: In the worked example, how did the second student open up the discourse around the paper?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How did the second student open up the discourse?

_items.text: They read it as one interpretation among several and advanced a reasoned reading of their own against the others.
_items.feedback: Yes. Admitting rival readings and arguing your own opens the discourse.

_items.text: They summarised the paper's interpretation and adopted it as established.
_items.feedback: That closes the discourse rather than opening it.

_items.text: They read the paper more carefully than the first student.
_items.feedback: Care alone does not open a discourse; admitting other readings does.

_items.text: They rejected the paper because it was only one source.
_items.feedback: Opening up a discourse engages the source, it does not dismiss it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Treating the paper as one reading among several, and arguing your own, opens the discourse.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that admitted other interpretations and added a reasoned voice.
_incorrect.final: The discourse was opened by reading the paper as one interpretation among several and advancing a reasoned reading. Adopting, re-reading or dismissing do not.

title: Formative check: justifying your reading
displayTitle: You are writing about a key source in {{context}}. Which approach best justifies your own reading as one creative voice in the debate?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach best justifies your reading as one voice in the debate?

_items.text: Set the source against rival interpretations in {{context}} and argue your reading from the evidence.
_items.feedback: Yes. Placing your reading against others, argued from evidence, is how you justify it in {{context}}.

_items.text: Adopt the source's interpretation because it is the most cited in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: Citation count does not settle a debate or justify a reading.

_items.text: Summarise the source as accurately as possible and add nothing further.
_items.feedback: An accurate summary reports; it does not advance your voice.

_items.text: Assert your reading strongly without reference to other interpretations.
_items.feedback: A reading justified against no alternatives is assertion, not argument.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you justify your reading by placing it against rivals and arguing from evidence.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that argues your reading against other interpretations.
_incorrect.final: A reading is justified by setting it against rivals in {{context}} and arguing from evidence. Deference, bare summary and assertion do not.

body: Why does creativity rank so highly among graduate attributes?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does creativity rank highly among graduate attributes?

_items.text: Because it generates workable options for problems that have no settled method.
_items.feedback: Yes. Creativity is problem-solving under uncertainty.

_items.text: Because it makes work longer and more varied.
_items.feedback: Length and variety are not the attribute.

_items.text: Because it lets a graduate avoid hard problems.
_items.feedback: Creativity meets hard problems rather than avoiding them.

_items.text: Because it is a fixed trait that cannot be developed.
_items.feedback: It is treated as a developable attribute.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Creativity generates workable options under uncertainty.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what creativity does with a problem that has no routine solution.

body: Which of these best shows creativity argued as a graduate attribute rather than praised in general?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best shows creativity argued as an attribute?

_items.text: Naming a concrete problem with no routine solution and a new option for it, linked to adaptability.
_items.feedback: Yes. That locates creativity in a real problem and links it to adaptability.

_items.text: Saying creative people are an asset to any employer.
_items.feedback: That is generic praise, not an argument.

_items.text: Listing creativity among personal strengths without an example.
_items.feedback: A bare claim is generic.

_items.text: Describing creativity as an inborn personality trait.
_items.feedback: Trait-talk is the opposite of appraising the attribute.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Locating creativity in a concrete problem, linked to adaptability, argues it as an attribute.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that ties creativity to a real problem.

body: A learning strategy you rely on has clearly stalled. Which response best shows creative self-regulation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response best shows creative self-regulation?

_items.text: Work out what the strategy is failing to do, then devise a different approach aimed at that gap.
_items.feedback: Yes. Diagnosing the gap and devising an alternative is the creative, self-regulating move.

_items.text: Put in more hours on the same strategy.
_items.feedback: Intensifying a stalled strategy is not amending it.

_items.text: Avoid the task so the strategy is not needed.
_items.feedback: Avoidance does not solve the strategy problem.

_items.text: Keep the strategy because it worked before.
_items.feedback: Past success does not help once it has stalled.

_feedback.correct: That's right. You diagnose the gap and devise a better route.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that changes the strategy in response to the stall.

body: Where in the self-regulated learning cycle does creative strategy-switching mainly belong?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Where in the cycle does strategy-switching belong?

_items.text: At monitoring and amending, once results show the strategy has stalled.
_items.feedback: Yes. The switch belongs where monitoring reveals a stall.

_items.text: Only at the very start, before any strategy is chosen.
_items.feedback: Switching responds to results that appear once a strategy runs.

_items.text: At no point; one strategy should be kept throughout.
_items.feedback: The cycle depends on amending a failing strategy.

_items.text: Only after the course is over.
_items.feedback: Amendment happens during the cycle.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The switch belongs at monitoring and amending.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. When does the cycle tell you a switch is needed?

body: What does it mean to open up the discourse around a source?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to open up the discourse around a source?

_items.text: To treat it as one interpretation among several and argue your own reading against the others.
_items.feedback: Yes. Admitting rival readings and arguing your own opens the discourse.

_items.text: To summarise its interpretation and adopt it as established.
_items.feedback: That closes the discourse.

_items.text: To reject it because it is only one source.
_items.feedback: Opening up engages the source rather than dismissing it.

_items.text: To read it several times until you agree with it.
_items.feedback: Care alone does not open a discourse.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Opening up means admitting other readings and arguing your own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that admits other interpretations.

body: To say that scholarly interpretation is creative is to say that it...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: To say scholarly interpretation is creative is to say that it...

_items.text: reads material imaginatively to argue meaning, defended against evidence and rival readings.
_items.feedback: Yes. Interpretation is disciplined imagination, answerable to evidence.

_items.text: invents findings the source does not contain.
_items.feedback: Creative interpretation does not fabricate.

_items.text: restates the source's conclusion as accurately as possible.
_items.feedback: That is description.

_items.text: avoids taking any position so as to stay neutral.
_items.feedback: Interpretation advances a reading.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Creative interpretation argues a reading imaginatively yet answerably.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Creative here means disciplined imagination, not invention or restatement.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: creativity as a graduate attribute, creative self-regulation, and creativity in scholarly discourse. On their own they can seem like three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one deliberate practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: By now you meet all three of these moves in your own work. The aim here is to see them as one deliberate creative practice rather than three separate ideas. That way creativity becomes something you direct on purpose, across your studies and into your professional life.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together creativity as an attribute, as self-regulation and as scholarly practice into one deliberate move
recognise that single creative practice at work in an experienced student's study
plan how you will exercise creativity as one practice across your {{context}} study and work

title: Concept: definition
body: Deliberate creative practice is one move you make on purpose, again and again. You meet a problem that has no settled method, generate a new and workable option, adapt it as things become clearer, and defend it with reasons. The three lessons are three arenas for that single move. Lesson one met it in professional problems, lesson two in your own learning, and lesson three in reading a source.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this one creative move turns up wherever a task has no set answer. You might face it in a problem at work, in a study strategy that has stalled, or in a source everyone treats as settled. The move is the same each time: generate a workable option, adapt it, and defend it with reasons.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one project or task ahead of you where no method is simply given. How might you generate a new option, adapt it and defend it, and when would you use that move again?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Creativity is most useful when you treat it as one deliberate practice. The same move serves you whether the problem is professional, your own learning, or a scholarly source: generate a new option, adapt it, and defend it. It is the single practice, not any one use of it, that strengthens your work across your studies.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Deliberate creative practice is one move you make on purpose, again and again. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Notice
_items.body: Notice a problem in your work that has no routine answer.

_items.title: Generate
_items.body: Generate a new, workable option rather than more of the same.

_items.title: Adapt
_items.body: Adapt the option as the constraints become clearer.

_items.title: Defend and review
_items.body: Defend your choice with reasons, then review how it went, which feeds the next problem you notice.

_diagram.title: Deliberate creative practice as one repeating move

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two experienced students meet the same three challenges in a term: a problem with no set method, a study routine that has stalled, and a source they had taken as settled. One treats each as a separate hurdle and handles them differently. The other sees one creative move behind all three, and applies it each time: generate an option, adapt it, defend it. By the end, the second student works with far more confidence.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep creativity as one practice
body: Use these to keep the single creative practice turning across your work, rather than treating each task as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I named the problem that has no settled method, rather than reaching for a familiar answer?
Have I generated a genuinely new option, not just more of the same?
Have I stayed ready to adapt the option as things become clearer?
Have I defended my choice with reasons, rather than asserting it?
Have I used the same move across my studies, not only in one task?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat creativity as one deliberate practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it more useful to treat creativity as one deliberate practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat creativity as one deliberate practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because the same move runs through all three: generate a new, workable option where no method is given, then adapt and defend it.
_items.feedback: Yes. One move, exercised in three arenas, is easier to direct on purpose than three separate ideas.

_items.text: Because learning three ideas separately is always harder than learning one.
_items.feedback: The point is not difficulty. It is that the three are really one move in different settings.

_items.text: Because only one of the three ideas was ever worth keeping.
_items.feedback: All three matter. Seeing them as one practice is what makes them usable.

_items.text: Because a single practice means you never have to adapt your approach.
_items.feedback: Adapting the option is part of the practice, not something it lets you skip.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three lessons are three arenas for one creative move, so treating it as a single practice lets you direct it on purpose.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the three lessons have in common as a single move.

displayTitle: A researcher meets a stubborn problem, amends a stalled method, and argues a fresh reading of a key source, all in one project. What does this show?
body: A researcher meets a stubborn problem, amends a stalled method, and argues a fresh reading of a key source, all in one project. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A researcher meets a stubborn problem, amends a stalled method, and argues a fresh reading of a key source, all in one project. What does this show?

_items.text: That creativity is one practice at work across the project: the same move of generating and defending a new option, in three different places.
_items.feedback: Yes. Attribute, self-regulation and scholarship are three faces of one creative practice.

_items.text: That the researcher was using three unrelated skills that happened to coincide.
_items.feedback: They are not unrelated. Each is the same creative move in a different arena.

_items.text: That creativity only counts when it appears in formal research.
_items.feedback: Creativity as one practice runs through everyday study too, not only research.

_items.text: That amending a method and reading a source have nothing to do with creativity.
_items.feedback: Both are creative moves: generating a better option and a fresh reading.

_feedback.correct: Correct. One creative practice showed up as an attribute, as self-regulation and as scholarship, all in a single piece of work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the same creative move appears in each part of the project.

displayTitle: You want to use creativity as one practice to work on {{context}} better this term. Which plan best treats creativity as one deliberate practice?
body: You want to use creativity as one practice to work on {{context}} better this term. Which plan best treats creativity as one deliberate practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use creativity as one practice to work on your subject better this term. Which plan best treats creativity as one deliberate practice?

_items.text: When a task has no routine answer, generate a new option, adapt it as you learn more, and defend your choice, in each piece of work.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the one creative move, repeated across the term.

_items.text: Wait for inspiration to strike, and only act creatively when it does.
_items.feedback: The practice is deliberate, not a matter of waiting for inspiration.

_items.text: Use a new approach once, early on, and then keep repeating it unchanged.
_items.feedback: Repeating it unchanged skips the adapting and defending that keep it creative.

_items.text: Keep your method fixed, so your work stays consistent all term.
_items.feedback: A fixed method is the opposite of the practice: it never generates a new option.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Spotting where no method is given, generating an option, adapting it and defending it keeps creativity working as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps the creative move deliberate and repeats it across the term.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Across this course, creativity appeared as an attribute, as self-regulation and as scholarship. What best describes how they relate?
body: Across this course, creativity appeared as an attribute, as self-regulation and as scholarship. What best describes how they relate?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Across this course, creativity appeared as an attribute, as self-regulation and as scholarship. What best describes how they relate?

_items.text: They are three arenas for one creative move: generate a new, workable option and defend it.
_items.feedback: Yes. One practice, three arenas.

_items.text: They are three unrelated skills with little in common.
_items.feedback: They share one move at their core.

_items.text: They are three names for exactly the same task done the same way.
_items.feedback: Same move, but three different settings.

_items.text: They are three stages you must complete in a fixed order.
_items.feedback: They are arenas for one move, not a fixed sequence.

_feedback.correct: Correct. One creative practice, exercised in three different arenas.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student hits a dead end in a project, drops a method that has stalled, and argues a new reading of a core source. Which best names what they are doing?
body: A student hits a dead end in a project, drops a method that has stalled, and argues a new reading of a core source. Which best names what they are doing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student hits a dead end in a project, drops a method that has stalled, and argues a new reading of a core source. Which best names what they are doing?

_items.text: Exercising creativity as one practice across the whole project.
_items.feedback: Yes. The same creative move, used in three places.

_items.text: Giving up on the project because the first method failed.
_items.feedback: Amending a method is not giving up; it is the creative move.

_items.text: Three separate skills that happen to appear together by chance.
_items.feedback: They are one move in three settings, not chance.

_items.text: Avoiding creativity by sticking to familiar methods.
_items.feedback: The student changed approach, which is the practice at work.

_feedback.correct: Correct. The same creative move, used in three places in one piece of work.
